title: Latency Attribution Scratchpad
content:
Purpose:
This is a working scratchpad for triaging short-term latency regressions that don't yet qualify as incidents. Focus: rapid attribution (what changed, where tokens are spent), low-friction bisects, and quick canary vs baseline comparisons to decide whether to roll back or let a canary complete.

High-level workflow (one-pager):
- Detect: alert fires (p95 or p99 > SLO for route/model).
- Quick triage (10–20m): determine scope (route, model, region, tier).
- Snapshot metrics: capture canary vs baseline windows, collect flamegraphs/pprof/KV-cache stats.
- Hypothesize cause(s): batching, kernel change, network, pre/post-processing, KV cache misses, quantization fallback.
- Bisect target: code, model version, infra kernel, container image.
- Decide: rollback canary, patch, or monitor more.

Checklist: initial 15m
- Which route(s) affected? (Grafana route-map panel)
- Is the spike correlated to a deploy? (Deploys panel: last 60m)
- Is it isolated to a region/availability zone? (region latency heatmap)
- Is error rate elevated? If yes, prioritize error triage first.
- Snapshot p50/p95/p99, token-cost breakdown, and request volume for both baseline and canary windows.
- Capture a short sample of request traces (trace IDs + top N call spans).

Queries / panels I run (examples):
- Prometheus p99: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, route, model))
- Token path cost (derived metric): sum(token_compute_ms) by (route, model) / sum(tokens)
- KV cache hit rate: sum(kv_cache_hits) / (sum(kv_cache_hits)+sum(kv_cache_misses)) by (model, pool)
- Batching depth distribution: histogram of requests per batch over 10m windows (custom metric batch.size)

Fast artifacts to capture for a triage snapshot (store as links in incident):
- Grafana dashboard snapshot (p50/p95/p99 + request rate) for baseline window (T-30m to T-15m) and impacted window (T0-15m to T0).
- 3 representative traces (one short, one medium, one long) exported from Jaeger with spans labeled: preproc, encode, attention-kernel, kv-lookup, postproc.
- One pprof flamegraph of worker process pinned to the same time window.
- Kernel logs: nvidia-smi, dmesg (for GPU OOMs), driver version.
- Model artifact version and container image tag.

Common root-cause buckets (with quick checks):
- Model change or weights: check model_version tag on traces and model catalog entry; run inference locally against the new version with a fixed prompt set to compare token timing.
- Serving code change (runtime): check deploy diff, look for batching/queue changes, KV cache PRs. Quick bisect: roll back last runtime image.
- Infrastructure (instance type, kernel, CUDA): compare gpu kernel versions in canary vs baseline and look for increased GPU utilization or memory pressure.
- Cold KV cache: sudden increase in kv_cache_misses + higher end-to-end latency. Check shard-level cache warmup metrics.
- Batching shift: changes in request arrival distribution can increase mean batch sizes and head-of-line waits. Look at batch.size distribution.

Bisect plan templates (pick one depending on suspected domain):
1) Code bisect (runtime):
  - If last deploy hash X corresponds to the time window, trigger rollback of that deploy in canary namespace.
  - If rollback resolves latency within 5m, open rollback PR and annotate cause.
  - If not, re-deploy baseline image but preserve canary traffic while you bisect further.

2) Model bisect:
  - Pin traffic back to previous model_version and observe. If latency drops, suspect model weighting or forward pass changes (longer seq, different attention config).
  - Run A/B microbench: local perf harness for small prompt set (10–100 requests) comparing versions and capture per-layer timings.

3) Infra kernel/driver bisect:
  - Compare node pools (old driver vs new). Temporarily re-route a fraction of traffic to node pool with older driver (if available).
  - If not available, repro in a dev cluster with same hardware driver combo.

What a “good” canary comparison looks like:
- Traffic split: 5/95 for at least 15min, then 20/80 for additional 15min if stable.
- Signal acceptance: p95 within 10% of baseline and p99 within 15% (absolute thresholds applied).
- No increase in error rate > 0.2% absolute or 50% relative.
- KV cache hit rate not decreased by >5% absolute.

Investigation notes (real examples / scratch):
- 2024-02-28 09:12: alert: p99 for route /chat-stream jumped from 240ms -> 410ms (NYC region). Deploy at 08:55 to canary-target-3.
  - Quick snapshot: batch.size median increased 1.8x; kv_cache_miss increased from 2.4% -> 11.5%; GPU util steady.
  - Hypothesis: cache key schema change in model-serving v2.31 caused cache miss storm; result: longer attention recompute across whole sequence.
  - Action: route canary back to baseline model_version and monitor. After rollback p99 returned to 260ms within 7m.
  - Follow-up: open PR to fix cache key generation (GH #422), add regression test that simulates KV key namespace change.

- 2024-01-18 14:00: minor drift: p95 up by ~12% across many routes; no single deploy in the window.
  - Observed: batching depth median decreased (more single-request batches), token-level cost per request increased.
  - Hypothesis: frontend traffic shaping changes introduced jitter in request arrival.
  - Action: adjusted autoscale watermarks and re-tuned batching window heuristic. p95 normalized in 48h.

Diagnostics commands I keep handy:
- tail -n 200 /var/log/serving-runtime/worker.log | grep "latency"
- go tool pprof -http=:8085 /tmp/profile.pb.gz   # open flamegraph
- jq -r '.spans[] | {name, duration_ms, tags}' trace.json | column -t
- redis-cli INFO | grep -E "hits|misses|keys"

Unresolved questions / TODOs:
- Add a prebuilt flamegraph upload playbook in infra-artifacts so on-call can attach one-click snapshots to alerts.
- Should we add an automated canary comparator job that fails if p99 increases > 12%? (Pros: faster rollbacks. Cons: noisy for non-deterministic workloads.)
- Create a synthetic prompt set focused on KV-sensitive workloads to run as part of every canary.

Quick wins to reduce future triage time:
- Standardize and shorten trace span names so that triage scripts can automatically match critical spans (preproc, kv-lookup, attention, softmax, postproc).
- Add mini-benchmark endpoints that execute the exact model forward pass used by route (no networking) to isolate pure compute regressions.
- Dashboard badge: show canary vs baseline p99 delta in the header for each route.

Notes to self: keep this doc minimal and chaotic — the point is to capture ephemeral hypotheses and actions. Move stable procedures into the canonical playbook when proven reproducible.

Recent links / artifacts (examples):
- Grafana snapshot baseline: https://grafana.redwood/snapshot/abc123
- Jaeger traces: https://jaeger.redwood/trace/def456
- GH PR to fix kv key: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/422

If you are triaging: ping @engin-team in #perf-alerts, include the short snapshot above (baseline window, impacted window, 3 traces, flamegraph link, suspected bucket).

End of scratchpad.  (Update: move verified patterns into /playbooks/if-stable.)
